quiz.q: Does Rust's standard library include regex support?
options: Yes, in std::regex
No — the regex crate is the ecosystem standard
Yes, but only for ASCII text
Only on the nightly compiler
quiz.explain: std has no regex engine at all. The regex crate, backed by a linear-time engine, is what the ecosystem reaches for.

quiz.q: Why should you compile a `Regex` once and reuse it, instead of calling `Regex::new` inside a loop?
options: Regex::new is deprecated
Compiling the pattern is the expensive part; recompiling every iteration wastes that work over and over
Rust doesn't allow Regex::new inside loops
A Regex value can only be used once and then must be discarded
quiz.explain: Compiling a pattern into a matching engine costs meaningfully more than running a match — always compile once and reuse.

quiz.q: Why does `Regex::new` need a raw string like `r"\d{4}"` instead of `"\d{4}"`?
options: Raw strings execute faster at runtime
Without r"", Rust tries to interpret \d as its own escape sequence and rejects it at compile time
Regex patterns must be written in all uppercase
It's purely a style convention with no real effect on compilation
quiz.explain: \d isn't a valid Rust string escape, so a plain string literal fails to compile before the regex engine ever sees the pattern. r"" makes backslashes literal.

quiz.q: What does a named capture group like `(?<year>\d{4})` let you do?
options: Nothing extra — it behaves identically to an unnamed group
Pull out the match by name (&caps["year"]) instead of a fragile numeric index
Make the regex engine run measurably faster
Force the match to be case-insensitive
quiz.explain: Named groups read better and stay correct if the pattern's groups are later reordered — a numeric index like &caps[1] would silently break.

options: The matched text itself
A bool
A Vec of every match
An Option<Captures>
quiz.explain: is_match() only answers yes/no. Use .find() for the matched text or .captures() for its labeled pieces.

quiz.q: Why might a regex pattern from Python or JavaScript fail to port directly to Rust's `regex` crate?
options: Rust's regex crate uses an entirely different syntax for digits and letters
Rust's regex crate deliberately doesn't support backreferences or lookaround, to guarantee linear-time matching
Rust regexes can only match ASCII text
Rust's regex crate requires every pattern to use named groups
quiz.explain: Leaving out backreferences/lookaround avoids catastrophic backtracking, guaranteeing linear-time matching — but it means some patterns from other engines need rewriting.

quiz.q: Which is the more idiomatic way to check if a path ends with ".rs"?
options: Regex::new(r"\.rs$").unwrap().is_match(path)
path.ends_with(".rs")
Both are equally idiomatic — pick whichever
Neither approach actually works for this
quiz.explain: A fixed suffix check doesn't need a pattern-matching engine — str::ends_with is clearer and needs no dependency.

quiz.q: What lets a `Regex` be compiled exactly once and reused everywhere without threading it through every function call?
options: A static std::sync::LazyLock<Regex> (or compiling once at startup)
Calling regex::Regex::clone() before each use
Creating a fresh Regex::new() call inside each function
Wrapping every call site in an unsafe block
quiz.explain: LazyLock builds the Regex the first time it's touched and reuses it for every call after that, avoiding the need to pass it around manually.

flashcards.back: No — the regex crate is the ecosystem standard, built on a linear-time (non-backtracking) engine.

flashcards.front: What's the expensive part of using a Regex?
flashcards.back: Compiling the pattern with Regex::new — always compile once and reuse the same Regex, never per-call or per-loop-iteration.

flashcards.front: Why do regex patterns need a raw string (r"...")?
flashcards.back: So backslashes reach the regex engine literally instead of being interpreted as Rust's own string escapes first.

flashcards.front: What does .captures() with a named group let you do?
flashcards.back: Extract a match by name, e.g. &caps["year"], instead of a fragile numeric index like &caps[1].

flashcards.front: What does the regex crate deliberately not support, and why?
flashcards.back: Backreferences and lookaround — leaving them out guarantees linear-time matching with no catastrophic backtracking.

flashcards.front: When should you reach for a plain str method instead of regex?
flashcards.back: When you're matching a fixed substring or doing a simple split — split_once, trim, starts_with, contains are clearer and need no dependency.

flashcards.front: How can you compile a Regex once and share it across your whole program?
flashcards.back: Store it in a static std::sync::LazyLock<Regex>, which builds it lazily on first use and reuses it after that.
